candidates.text:
Damn... this story hits heavy.

She asked him to stop initiating, he actually listened for *sixteen months*, no pressure, no sneaking, nothing. And then one day he’s like “yeah I’m done living like roommates.”

The quiet part is what gets me. He wasn’t yelling or cheating or making threats. He just slowly checked out while still showing up for the kid and the laundry. That’s the scary part is when the fighting stops because one person already left in their head.

Sixteen months of “I’ll tell you when I’m ready” with no timeline is a long time to keep hoping the connection comes back. You can’t take one of the biggest parts of marriage off the table indefinitely and act surprised when the other person eventually walks.

Painful story. Real one though.

candidates.text:
I'm now building an "improvements" feature into all of my personal vibecoded applications: a freeform text input that's hooked up to an agent that yolo implements whatever is submitted.

It's an interesting experience -- the activation energy barrier to sanding any rough edge or implementing any new feature becomes extremely low. Someone else who uses one of the applications I created has already implemented 150 improvements over the course of a few days. This pattern feels like a new kind of tool -- liquid software? -- and every application that doesn't have this feature now has a slightly rigid and anachronistic flavor. Why can't I just tell it how I want it to be different?

Now, it's not obvious to me how this pattern can or should scale. Does it become unmaintainable after a while? (Maybe model intelligence improvement outstrips my feature appetite such that it's fine?) How does collaborative software work in this model? Can software designed this way be secure and reliable?

Whatever the larger questions about broader deployment, it definitely works great in a personal context. It reminds me a little of the visions of Lisp/Lisp machines, Smalltalk, and HyperCard -- systems that the user can take control of and modify. Those visions never quite worked, though: the vast majority of software today is not end-user modifiable in any useful way. So, while this "liquid" affordance is a very small touch, the way it changes one's relation to the software feels a bit transgressive and empowering in a Lickliderian and Engelbartian way.

candidates.text:
Seeing a lot of mentions that Wispr made a mistake by educating its users about Granola. Maybe that's true but here's my take.

I worked in the productivity category for ~12 years across two startups (calendaring and meeting notes), both acquired.

Productivity startups rarely make it to IPO. The few examples such as Dropbox and Asana, you could argue haven't been great from a public market stock perspective. The challenge is that you're constantly battling the heavyweights, specifically Google and Microsoft, who are going to build a good-enough alternative and bundle it for basically free. Of course, CIOs love this. No buyer wants to manage 10 different SKUs when they can pay $15/seat and get all of it.

Now consumers, sure, some will pay and this drove early Dropbox, Evernote, Calendly, Granola subs but you do hit a ceiling. Eventually, new subscriber growth struggles to keep up with churn because consumers ultimately gravitate to free.

So your only choice as a productivity startup is to use that initial wedge, which I often describe as identifying an icon that doesn't exist in the Google Apps dashboard, and then expand horizontally. And in fact, this is precisely why Dropbox, Slack, Zoom or even Notion all continue to build or acquire more of the productivity suite.

Unfortunately, it’s impossibly hard. The incumbents aren't sitting idle, and they have huge pricing power because of scale. Ultimately, as a startup in this category, as a founder, you have at least 1 exit window, maybe 2 if you're lucky.

For sure companies like Miro, Airtable and others have likely had an attractive exit window but the founders went for it. Unclear if all that additional grinding led to a better outcome for the team and founders.

FWIW, at one of my productivity startups, I ended up selling three years after receiving our first acquisition offer. Three more years of grinding, more venture capital, more stress, and ultimately I walked away with roughly the same amount of cash I would have had if I'd sold two years in.

So the obvious Q is why does productivity continue to get so much venture funding if so few of these companies ever get to IPO? First, productivity is one of those evergreen categories where investors often experience the pain themselves and that’s a huge advantage in fundraising. Second, you can still make money as an investor as long as the money raised and valuations don’t get out of control. Like with anything, if you raise too much money, then there aren’t enough buyers.

This category though, maybe sees more acquisitions than others and the reason for that is because practically every large enterprise software company has, at some point, aspired to build its own version of Google Apps because who doesn’t want to own the backbone of enterprise? Most of these buyers though discover that it takes billions and years and so they ultimately give up and the cycle repeats some years later with new leaders.

So full circle, what's the playbook for Wispr and Granola? Well, first, they're both going to expand horizontally as quickly as possible. Second, they're going to invest in team editions and sell into enterprise. This is really the only way.

Finally, I wouldn’t be surprised if both are already getting acquisition offers but I’m also sure the founders have taken some liquidity, and so they are going to go for it.
